subject: Civil Engineering
title: Spinning Cables: How Main Cables Are Made
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Spinning Cables: How Main Cables Are Made.

hook.text: You can't ship an 80,000-mile cable. You spin it wire by wire on-site.

buildup.text: A spinning wheel carries one wire at a time from anchorage to anchorage, back and forth.

discovery.text: Thousands of parallel wires are bundled, compacted, and wrapped into the final cable.

twist.text: John Roebling invented aerial spinning for the Brooklyn Bridge in the 1870s.

climax.text: Modern prefabricated strand methods speed the process — entire bundles at a time.

punchline.text: The world's biggest cables are woven one thin wire at a time.

quiz.question: How are the main cables of suspension bridges typically constructed?
options: A single thick cable is manufactured in a factory and shipped whole
Individual wires are spun on-site, then bundled and compacted
Chains of linked steel bars are assembled on the ground and hoisted

details.summary: Main cables of suspension bridges are built wire by wire using aerial spinning, where a spinning wheel carries individual wires back and forth between anchorages over the towers.
details.whyItMatters: Cable spinning is one of civil engineering's most impressive construction processes. The technique, pioneered for the Brooklyn Bridge, has enabled every major suspension bridge built since.
takeaways: Aerial spinning carries individual wires between anchorages over towers
The Golden Gate Bridge's cables contain 27,572 wires each
Compacting and wrapping transforms loose wire bundles into solid cables

faq.question: How long does it take to spin the main cables of a suspension bridge?
faq.answer: Cable spinning for major suspension bridges typically takes 12 to 18 months of continuous operation. The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge's cables each contain 36,830 wires and took about 18 months to spin using multiple spinning wheels working simultaneously.

faq.question: What happens to suspension bridge cables as they age?
faq.answer: Wire corrosion from moisture penetrating the wrapping is the primary concern. Broken wires reduce cable capacity over decades. Engineers inspect cables by unwrapping sections and testing individual wires.
